questions.question_text:
Mr Jones is a 56-year-old man who is an inpatient on the surgical ward. His elective hernia repair has been delayed so he has been in
hospital fasted and waiting for 24 hours. He usually drinks 6-8 cans of lager a day. He has already started to experience a headache, anxiety
and mild tremor. With regards to acute alcohol withdrawal without delirium when are his symptoms likely to peak?
questions.explanation:
Most patients who drink excessive alcohol manifest a minor withdrawal syndrome, which may start as early as 6-8 hours after an abrupt
reduction in alcohol intake. It can include any combination of generalized hyperactivity, anxiety, tremor, sweating, nausea, tachycardia,
hypertension and mild pyrexia. These symptoms usually peak between 10 to 30 hours and subside by 40 to 50 hours. Seizures may occur in
the �rst 12 to 48 hours and only rarely after this. Auditory and visual hallucinations may develop; these are characteristically frightening and
may last for �ve to six days. NB: Delirium Tremens occurs usually 48-72 hours after cessation of drinking. (Reference: Alcohol Use Disorders:
Diagnosis and Clinical Management of Alcohol-Related Physical Complications [Internet]. NICE Clinical Guidelines, No. 100. National Clinical
Guideline Centre (UK). London: Royal College of Physicians (UK); 2010)

questions.question_text:
Mr David O‘Neill is a 52-year-old man who has a long history of alcohol dependence. Recently his family has noticed him "not being himself“
and has brought him to the GP. Which of the following area of the brain are most likely to be damaged by alcohol?
questions.explanation:
In terms of the degree of vulnerability to chronic alcohol related damage, diencephalic structures and cerebellum are the most a�ected (due
to thiamine disruption), followed by white matter damage, particulary a�ecting the genu of the corpus callosum. Working memory de�cits
relate to the damage sustained by the genu of the corpus callosum. While some patients exhibit cerebral cortical atrophy, this is usually a
later feature, seen in those with 'alcohol-related dementia‘. Ref: Sullivan EV, Harris RA, Pfe�erbaum A. Alcohol‘s e�ects on brain and
behavior. Alcohol Research & Health. 2010;33(1-2):127.

questions.question_text:
Max is a 44-year-old man with mild alcohol dependence without signi�cant physical sequelae. He is attending the local drug and alcohol
service for his �rst appointment with his partner. He asks for a pharmacological intervention to reduce his craving. Which of the following
treatment combinations should you o�er him?

options.text: Naltrexone and acceptance and commitment therapy

questions.explanation:
NICE guidelines state that for harmful drinkers and people with mild dependence who have not responded to psychological interventions, or
who request a pharmacological intervention consider o�ering acamprosate or naltrexone in combination with psychological intervention
(individual CBT, behavioural therapy, behavioural couples therapy, or social network and environmental therapies). Acceptance and
commitment therapy is not recommended in the NICE guidelines, and it is unlikely that anyone who is currently dependent on alcohol would
be appropriate for psychodynamic therapy. Methadone and buprenorphine are treatments for opiate dependence rather than alcohol so
are not correct. (Ref: NICE Guideline: [CG 115] (2011). Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis, assessment and management of harmful drinking
and alcohol dependence (1.3.3 Interventions for harmful drinking and mild alcohol dependence.)

questions.question_text:
Mr Colin Flood is a 43-year-old man with a long-standing history of alcohol misuse. He is brought to A&E by his friends as they are
concerned about him being unwell. He is later diagnosed with Wernicke‘s encephalopathy. Which of the following symptom clusters is he
most likely to have presented with?

options.text: Triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia and cerebellar signs

questions.explanation:
The most common symptom in Wernicke‘s is confusion, occurring in around 80% cases. Ophthalmoplegia occurs in around 30% of cases and
cerebellar signs in about 23%. Only around 10% of patients with Wernicke‘s encephalopathy present with the classical triad of symptoms.

questions.question_text:
Mr. Andrews is a 28 year old man who has presented to his local Emergency Department with frank blood in his urine and pain in his
abdomen. He informed sta� that he has recently used illicit drugs and is concerned that this may have caused his symptoms. Which of the
below illicit drugs is most likely to cause this presentation?
questions.explanation:
Ketamine can cause severe ulcerative cystitis, which presents with abdominal pain, frank haematuria, urinary frequency, urgency and
dysuria. In severe cases surgery, such as cystectomy is necessary. Up to 30% of chronic ketamine users can have urinary symptoms.

questions.question_text:
Mr Oliver Hirsh is a 24-year-old man who has a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia. He was brought to A&E by his family after he presented
as confused at home. In A&E he was found to be hyperthermic, tachycardic, hypertensive and showing signs of increased muscular re�exes.
He managed to inform the sta� that he took an overdose of Sertraline and Haloperidol earlier that day. Which of the following is the most
likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This is more likely to be Serotonin syndrome as the patient is presenting with rapid onset symptoms and hyperre�exia. Neuroleptic
malignant syndrome is associated with onset of symptoms over the course of days to weeks and characterized by muscular rigidity.
Anticholinergic toxicity is associated with profound visual impairment, urinary retention and marked constipation.

questions.question_text:
Mr Keith Viner is a 38-year-old man who has presented to his GP with a 6 week history of low mood, poor motivation, diminished sleep and
appetite, limited energy levels and feelings of despair about the future. He is willing to try medication but has heard that some psychiatric
medications can cause sexual side-e�ects, which he is keen to avoid. Which of the following are least likely to cause sexual side-e�ects?
questions.explanation:
Mirtazapine, Bupropion and Vortioxetine are the antidepressants least associated with sexual side-e�ects. Fewer than 10% of patients
taking Mirtazapine report di�culties. Around 70% of those taking SSRIs or Venlafaxine report symptoms. TCAs are signi�cantly associated
with sexual side-e�ects as well.

questions.question_text:
In your outpatient clinic you are seeing Miss Jackson, a 30-year-old teacher experiencing her �rst episode of depression. She has been
prescribed 40mg citalopram for 2 months with some improvement in sleep and appetite but she continues to have negative ruminations,
anxiety, suicidal thoughts, and is unable to concentrate and work. She has not had any other treatments for depression. She is on the
waiting list for CBT but this will likely not be available for some months. Which ONE of the following pharmacological treatments should you
o�er her today?

options.text: Switch to a di�erent SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor)

correct_answer.text: Switch to a di�erent SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor)

questions.explanation:
NICE guidelines recommend that when reviewing drug treatment for a person whose symptoms have not responded to initial
pharmacological interventions consideration should be given to switching to an alternative antidepressant. Checking compliance prior to
doing this is also important. NICE Guideline (CG90) 1.8.1.2 states: Consider switching to: initially a di�erent SSRI or a better tolerated newer-
generation antidepressant, subsequently an antidepressant of a di�erent pharmacological class that may be less well tolerated, for example
venlafaxine, a TCA or an MAOI Augmentation with another agent would not be appropriate initially but may be required if other treatments
are not successful. The maximum dose for citalopram is 40mg so increasing to 60mg is not advised, due to the risk of QT prolongation.
(Reference: Depression in adults: recognition and management, Clinical guideline [CG90]

questions.question_text:
Mr Jenkins is a 20-year-old man who is being reviewed in �rst seizure clinic. The neurologist suspects he su�ers from non-epileptic attacks
(or dissociative seizures) based on the history Mr Jenkins provides. Which ONE of the following patient reported seizure characteristics has
the best utility in di�erentiating non-epileptic attacks from epilepsy?

options.text: Biting the inside of the mouth
Recall for the period of unresponsiveness

correct_answer.text: Recall for the period of unresponsiveness

questions.explanation:
Although patients with Non-Epileptic Attacks (NEA) often report seizures in sleep, when they are captured on telemetry they are inevitably
preceded by waking, which again can be recorded electrographically. Thus patient report of seizures during sleep are not necessarily helpful
as discriminators and need to be examined further. The following are also not de�nitive discriminators: Biting the inside of the mouth occurs
occasionally in NEA and commonly in epilepsy. Incontinence can occasionally occur in NEA and occurs commonly in epilepsy. Stereotyped
attacks occur commonly in both NEA and epilepsy. Patients with NEA often have recall for their period of apparent unresponsiveness,
whereas those with epileptic seizures do not. Therefore of the above list, this is the best answer. (Reference: Mellers JD. The approach to
patients with "non-epileptic seizures“. Postgraduate medical journal. 2005 Aug 1;81(958):498-504).

questions.question_text:
Neurosurgery for mental disorders (NMD) is an uncommon treatment modality. NICE has suggested it in certain circumstances. Which of
the following disorders can be treated with NMD according to NICE guidelines?
questions.explanation:
Intractable OCD can be treated via neurosurgery if other treatment modalities have failed. NMD is rarely performed with only 4 procedures
carried out in 2015-16.

questions.question_text:
Miss Di�orio is a 39-year-old woman who is having outpatient treatment for her stable bipolar illness. She has read recently about gender
di�erences in mental health conditions and would like to know more about this with relevance to bipolar. Which ONE of the following
bipolar spectrum conditions or comorbidities has an equal gender distribution?
questions.explanation:
Previous studies and a review in 2010 report an almost equal gender ratio in the prevalence of bipolar disorder but the majority of studies
do report an increased risk in women of bipolar II/hypomania, rapid cycling and mixed a�ective episodes. Comorbidity; particularly thyroid
disease, migraine, obesity, and anxiety disorders occur more frequently in women than men, whilst substance use disorders are more
common in men. (References: Di�orio A, Jones I. Is sex important? Gender di�erences in bipolar disorder. International Review of Psychiatry.
2010 Oct 1;22(5):437-52. Arnold LM. Gender di�erences in bipolar disorder. The Psychiatric Clinics of North America. 2003 Sep;26(3):595-
620).

questions.question_text:
Miss Olivia Hunt is a 33-year-old woman with a diagnosis of obsessive compulsive disorder. She has recently received an adequate trial of
Sertraline 200mg daily and a course of CBT for 20 sessions. Unfortunately, this has made little di�erence to her symptoms. Which of the
following would be the most appropriate next step in her management?
questions.explanation:
The NICE guidelines indicate that if a patient has had an adequate trial of a combined SSRI and CBT then they should be o�ered a di�erent
SSRI or Clomipramine. If this is ine�ective, then further intensive CBT or a low dose antipsychotic can be o�ered.

questions.question_text:
John is 26 years old and has body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). He has been taking sertraline 200mg for the last three months and having
CBT but continues to spend hours of the day looking in the mirror. He has previously tried �uoxetine at maximum dose with minimal
bene�t. What is the best next step in treatment?

options.text: Switch from sertraline to another SSRI

questions.explanation:
NICE guidelines state BDD should be treated initially with CBT and then if symptoms are severe adding an SSRI. There is very limited
research on head to head trials for antidepressants or for treatment resistant BDD. The Maudsley guidelines suggest that buspirone may
augment the SSRI. (Ref: NICE Guidelines: Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment. Clinical guideline [CG31]
(2005). Available: Taylor, D., Paton, C. and Kapur, S. (n.d.). Anxiety Spectrum Disorders. The Maudsley prescribing guidelines in psychiatry. 12th ed. Chichester:
John Wiley & Sons, pp.355).

questions.question_text:
You are seeing a 25-year-old woman in outpatients for treatment of moderate depression. Which ONE of the following symptoms are
considered a core feature of depression?
questions.explanation:
A study of outpatients with either or major depression found that across all levels of severity some symptoms were present in 60% or more
of patients. The following are therefore considered core symptoms: Sad, irritable, or anxious mood, Loss of interest or pleasure, Impaired
concentration and decision making, Worthlessness and inappropriate guilt, Hopelessness, Fatigue or loss of energy. Panic attacks may occur
in depression with anxiety but are not a core feature. Talkativeness would suggest hypomania or mania. Auditory hallucinations can occur in
psychotic depression but are not a core feature of depression. All over body pain can occur in depression, especially in particular ethnic
groups but is not an agreed core symptom according to current criteria. (Ref: Rakofsky JJ, Schettler PJ, Kinkead BL, Frank E, Judd LL, Kupfer
DJ, Rush AJ, Thase ME, Yonkers KA, Rapaport MH. The prevalence and severity of depressive symptoms along the spectrum of unipolar
depressive disorders: a post hoc analysis. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2013 Nov;74(11):1084-91)

questions.question_text:
Mr Fox is a 60-year-old man who is taking lithium for stable bipolar disorder. He presents to A&E with confusion and falls in the context of a
recent chest infection. Which of the following features would be NOT be consistent with acute lithium toxicity?
questions.explanation:
Nystagmus, ataxia, sluggishness, agitation, fasciculations and coarse tremor are neurological features of lithium toxicity. Reported cardiac
e�ects are QTc prolongation and bradycardia. Fever is not seen in lithium toxicity and would suggest sepsis or the need to consider
neuroleptic malignant syndrome, depending on the other symptoms. (Ref: Perrone J, Chatterjee P. Lithium poisoning.  uptodate.
com. Wolters Kluwer Health. 2015:1-3)

questions.question_text:
Mrs Carol Anwar is a 40-year-old woman who has a diagnosis of HIV and a history of having di�culty taking her antiretrovirals regularly. She
has been admitted to A&E in a confused and feverish state. Her MRI scan shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Which of the following is
the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Multiple ring enhancing lesions on MRI in patients with a diagnosis of HIV tend to indicate either CNS toxoplasmosis or CNS lymphoma. The
two are generally distinguished by CT scan.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Tara Neville is a 32-year-old woman with a diagnosis of schizophrenia. She has been well for 3 years and she and her husband are
planning on having children. She is wondering what the risk of them developing schizophrenia would be. Which of the following would be
the most appropriate answer?
questions.explanation: Studies indicate that children have a risk of around 9-14% of developing schizophrenia if one of their parents has the diagnosis.

questions.question_text:
A young male patient on the acute psychiatric ward is known to have non-epileptic attacks. After a ward round he is observed in the
common area on the sofa with jerky movements and appearing to have an attack. Which ONE the following features are more likely to
suggest that this is an epileptic rather than a non-epileptic attack?

options.text: Impaired ability to recall the attack
Side to side head movements during attack
Evidence of visual �xation during the attack
Downgoing plantar re�exes after the attack
Resistance to eye opening during the attack

correct_answer.text: Impaired ability to recall the attack

questions.explanation:
Side to side head movements and resistance to eye opening are more common in Non-Epileptic Attacks. Neurological testing during a Non-
Epileptic Attack will �nd that visual �xation is present (whereas it is not in an epileptic attack). Plantars are often up-going after an epileptic
attack and should be normal after a non-Epileptic Attack. Inability to recall the attack and post-ictal confusion is suggestive of an epileptic
attack. (Ref: Mellers JD. The approach to patients with "non-epileptic seizures“. Postgraduate medical journal. 2005 Aug 1;81(958):498-504)

questions.question_text:
Which ONE mood-stabilizing medication used in bipolar is associated with the greatest reduction in risk of attempted and completed
suicide?
questions.explanation:
Around 15% of people with bipolar complete suicide. Meta-analyses of clinical trials have demonstrated that lithium reduced the risk of both
attempted and completed suicide. Two large database studies have shown that patients taking lithium were less likely to complete suicide
than those treated with valproate, valproic acid or other mood stabilizing drugs such as gapabentin or carbamazepine. (Ref: Taylor, D.,
Paton, C. and Kapur, S. (n.d.). Chapter 3: Bipolar a�ective disorder. The Maudsley prescribing guidelines in psychiatry. 12th ed. Chichester:
John Wiley & Sons, pp.190)

questions.question_text:
Numerous risk factors have been identi�ed for the development of schizophrenia. Which of the following is most likely to place an individual
at risk of developing schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Migration has been consistently associated with the development of schizophrenia.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Lisa Lodge is a 34-year-old woman who is 2 months post-partum. Her health visitor notices that she is presenting as low in mood
struggling to bond with her baby. She administers the Edinburgh Post-natal Depression Scale. Which of the following is true regarding this
tool?

options.text: It recommended that it is used at 4 months post-partum
It has only been validated in the post-partum period
It can be used for diagnosis

questions.explanation:
A high score on the EPNDS predicts suicidality, particularly if the patient answers positively to question 10: "the thought of harming myself
has occurred to me“. It has been conceptualised as measuring depressive, anxiety and anhedonia symptoms and has been validated for use
in pregnancy and even in general population. It is a screening tool and higher scores can indicate a wide range of possible diagnoses. It is
generally used at 6-8 weeks post-partum.

questions.question_text:
Many mental health conditions are more prevalent amongst males or females. Which of the following has equal prevalence for males and
females?
questions.explanation:
Social phobia has equal prevalence for males and females in community samples. In clinic samples males have typically been over-
represented.

questions.question_text:
Jackie is a 24-year-old woman who is recovering from her �rst episode of psychosis where she was treated with risperidone. She has gained
more than 10kg in the last 3 months since starting treatment and now has raised lipids. She is wondering if she can change to another
antipsychotic. Which ONE of the following antipsychotics has the least potential to cause metabolic syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Clozapine and olanzapine all have a high risk of weight gain and metabolic syndrome. Quetiapine, Paliperidone and Chlorpromazine have a
moderate risk. Aripiprazole has low risk for weight gain and metabolic syndrome. (Ref: Taylor, D., Paton, C. and Kapur, S. (n.d.). Antipsychotic
induced weight gain. The Maudsley prescribing guidelines in psychiatry. 12th ed. Chichester: John Wiley & Sons, pp.90)

questions.question_text:
Mr Ross Giles is a 32-year-old man with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia who has recently started taking Clozapine. He
reports to his care co-ordinator that he has been feeling generally unwell and they arrange for him to have some blood tests. His
neutrophils are 5 x109/L and his CRP is 60mg/L. You are the doctor on duty for the team. Which would be the next most appropriate
investigation?
questions.explanation:
General malaise and a high CRP in the context of starting Clozapine raise the possibility of myocarditis which is a serious but rare side-e�ect.
This is particularly the case in the absence of any evidence of a speci�c source of infection or other in�ammation. Myocarditis must be ruled
out in the �rst instance as it can be fatal if not identi�ed and treated promptly.

questions.question_text:
Jane is a 15-year-old girl currently admitted under the mental health act to an adolescent unit. She is having her �rst episode of mania with
psychotic features, having previously had a history of depression and been prescribed �uoxetine. Which ONE of the following would be
appropriate as a single agent in treatment of Jane's mania?
questions.explanation:
Recommended �rst line treatments for acute mania in children and adolescents include atypical antipsychotics such as aripiprazole,
olanzapine, quetiapine and risperidone. Lithium can be used but would not be appropriate for Jane as a monotherapy as she has psychotic
symptoms. Carbamazepine is not recommended. Sodium Valproate has not shown e�cacy in a small RCT for adolescent mania. (Reference:
Taylor, D., Paton, C. and Kapur, S. (n.d.). Bipolar illness in children and adolescents. The Maudsley prescribing guidelines in psychiatry. 12th
ed. Chichester: John Wiley & Sons, pp.364-365).

questions.question_text:
James is a 17-year-old boy who was diagnosed with ADHD at the age of 8. He is seeing you in CAMHS and has asked about the
neurobiological basis of his illness. He is aware the fronto-striatal network is implicated. Which brain region does NOT form part of the
fronto-striatal network?
questions.explanation:
Data from neuroimaging, neuropsychology, neurochemistry and genetics consistently implicate the fronto-striatal network as a major
contributor to the pathophysiology of ADHD. The network involves the lateral prefrontal cortex, the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, the
caudate nucleus and putamen. The cerebellum is not part of the network. (Ref: Emond V, Joyal C, Poissant H. Structural and functional
neuroanatomy of attention-de�cit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). L‘encéphale. 2009 Apr;35(2):107-14).

questions.question_text:
Mr Neil Slater is a 16-year-old boy with a diagnosis of autistic spectrum disorder. He attends a special school and is soon to go to college.
What is the likelihood that he would also have a diagnosis of epilepsy?
questions.explanation:
A recent study suggested that 22% of people with an autism spectrum disorder develop epilepsy by the age of 21 years. This is in keeping
with previous studies. (Ref: Bolton PF, Carcani-Rathwell I, Hutton J, Goode S, Howlin P, Rutter M. Epilepsy in autism: features and correlates.
The British Journal of Psychiatry. 2011 Apr;198(4):289-94.)

questions.question_text:
Miss Joan Sta�ord is a 15-year-old girl who has been su�ering from persistent low mood, reduced interest in activities, irritability, poor sleep
and appetite, and diminishing school performance. She has had a trial of CBT which was not e�ective. Her parents are not willing for her to
have any medications. Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step for her treatment?
questions.explanation:
NICE guidelines for treatment of depression in children and adolescents' states that if a trial of an initial psychological intervention is
unsuccessful, an alternative, such of CBT, interpersonal therapy or family therapy should be considered. Fluoxetine can also be considered if
the patient or carers are accepting of this. Repeating a therapy that has been ine�ective would not be helpful and counselling is unlikely to
be successful if a formal psychotherapy has not worked. Individual psychotherapy and systemic family therapy are generally o�ered after
two trials of psychotherapy has been unsuccessful.

questions.question_text:
Oliver is a 10-year-old boy who sustained a head injury falling from his skateboard 2 months ago. At the time he lost consciousness for less
than 1 minute and had a GCS of 14 when he was later seen in A&E. He had some vomiting which settled within 24 hours of the injury. You
are now seeing him 2 months later in CAMHS and his mother is wondering if there is a link between the head injury and his current
complaint. Which ONE of the following neuropsychiatric syndromes or symptoms is NOT associated with mild Traumatic Brain Injury (mTBI)
in children?
questions.explanation:
A systematic review found consistent associations between mTBI and ADHD, conduct disorder, depression and anxiety. However the review
did suggest that the lack of pre-injury reports make �rm conclusions di�cult. Mania has not been reported. (Ref: Emery CA, Barlow KM,
Brooks BL, Max JE, Villavicencio-Requis A, Gnanakumar V, Robertson HL, Schneider K, Yeates KO. A systematic review of psychiatric,
psychological, and behavioural outcomes following mild traumatic brain injury in children and adolescents. The Canadian Journal of
Psychiatry. 2016 May;61(5):259-69).

questions.question_text:
Andrew Davies is a 9-year-old boy who has a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder. His mother has noticed that sometimes he can
comment on individual aspects of an object but not seem to see it as a ‘whole'. She gives the example of him being able to talk about wheels
on a toy car but not being able to identify its overall shape. Which of the following best describes this phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Central coherence theory underlies the central disturbance seen in people with autistic spectrum disorders. It is considered as a speci�c
perceptual-cognitive style. It is loosely described as a limited ability to understand context or to "see the big picture".

questions.question_text:
Forensic psychiatrists, as with other specialists within mental health, consider various factors when formulating the di�culties of their
patients, including organic ones. Damage to which of the following areas of the brain would a forensic psychiatrist be most interested in?
questions.explanation:
Damage to the frontal lobe is associated with a variety of symptoms relating to executive functioning and personality. The prefrontal cortex
is particularly associated with impulse control which is potentially relevant to forensic psychiatrists.

questions.question_text:
Mr James Bulwell is a 32-year-old man who has been serving a life sentence for murder. He has developed a psychotic illness during his time
in prison. He is presenting as chaotic and requires treatment. Which of the following would be the most appropriate venue for his
treatment?
questions.explanation:
It would be most appropriate for him to be transferred to a medium secure forensic ward, although he may require high secure depending
upon his presentation and risk history. It is unlikely that he could be managed in the prison if he is chaotic as the ability to deliver treatment
to an incapacitous patient is limited. A general psychiatric ward would be inappropriate due the degree of risk. As would a PICU as they are
usually only considered to be low secure.

questions.question_text:
Con�dentiality is an important concept in psychiatry, and general medical, practice. Which of the following cases refers to matters around
con�dentiality?
questions.explanation:
The Taraso� case relates to con�dentiality. Tatiana Taraso� was murdered by a classmate at college who had previously indicated to a
psychologist that he had a plan to kill her. The psychologist had not disclosed this information to the authorities or Tatiana Taraso�. It led to
court judgements in 1974 and 1976 that health professionals had a duty to breach con�dentiality in cases when they are aware of a realistic
threat to others.

questions.question_text:

health in prisons is true?

options.text: Personality disorder is the most common diagnosis

Most non-violent o�enders are not dependent on alcohol

The prevalence of schizophrenia in the prison population is similar to the general population.

correct_answer.text: Personality disorder is the most common diagnosis

questions.explanation:
Personality disorder, particularly antisocial PD is the most common diagnosis among prison populations. There is signi�cant overlap
between the diagnostic criteria for this and the factors that would lead to incarceration.

questions.question_text:
Mr Barlow is a 35-year-old man who has just been convicted of GBH, common assault and theft. He will be sentenced to 9 years in prison.
He has asked to see the prison psychiatrist following his initial intake review. Regarding the male prison population as a whole, what is the
most prevalent mental disorder?
questions.explanation:
The estimated prevalence of antisocial PD is 47%, of alcohol misuse or dependence 18-30%, posttraumatic stress disorder 4-21%,
depression 10%, and psychosis 4%. (Source: Ginn, S. Dealing with mental disorder in prisoners BMJ 2012; 345 :e7280)

questions.question_text:
Mr. Young is a 28-year-old man with a diagnosis of schizophrenia who is currently under the mental health act in a medium secure unit. He
is repeatedly presenting as 'aggressive‘. Which of the following would be the most e�ective method to manage his behaviour?
questions.explanation:
E�ective treatment of his underlying psychotic illness would be the most e�ective way to reduce aggressive behaviour. There is some
evidence that clozapine may be superior to other antipsychotics in terms of managing aggression.

questions.question_text:
Mental health problems and violent o�ending are often highlighted by the media and described by the public as a concern. Which of the
following statements about mental health and violence is true?

options.text: 70% of mental health patients who commit crimes are dependent on alcohol
People with a mental health problem are more likely to be the victim of violent crime than be the perpetrator
Patients with a substance dependence disorder are as likely to be assaulted as those without
If a mental health problem is associated with violence, e�ective treatment does not in�uence the risk to others
People with a mental health problem are more likely to commit violent crimes than those without

correct_answer.text: People with a mental health problem are more likely to be the victim of violent crime than be the perpetrator

questions.explanation:
People with mental health problems are far more likely to be the victims of violent crime than perpetrators. Schizophrenia and other
psychoses can be associated with increased rates of violence towards others, but this is still less likely than them being victims.

questions.question_text:
Mental health problems are more common in o�ending populations. Which of the following is the most common psychiatric disorder
among homicide o�enders?
questions.explanation:
9% of people convicted of homicide had a diagnosis of personality disorder. The �gures for other disorders were: schizophrenia – 5%;
a�ective disorder – 7%; alcohol dependence – 7%; drug dependence – 6%.

questions.question_text:
Mr Elsworth is a 39-year-old man who is an inmate in a category B prison following a sexual o�ence. He undergoes a risk assessment,
accounting for historical and psychological factors that would in�uence the probability of him o�ending again. Which of the following factors
would increase the risk of sexual reo�ending the most?

options.text: Dissocial personality disorder and Paedophilic paraphilia
Sexual assault with penetration of a stranger

correct_answer.text: Dissocial personality disorder and Paedophilic paraphilia

questions.explanation:
O�enders who demonstrate a persistent lack of empathy and guilt, as in dissocial personality disorder, and who demonstrate evidence of
sexual deviance, such as paedophilia, are most likely to sexually reo�end. Those who sexually assault strangers, and particularly those who
commit rape, are likely to reo�end as well, but show more general criminal behaviour and will commit other violent o�ences.

questions.question_text:
Ganser syndrome is a rare mental disorder, which presents with a particular set of symptoms. Which of the following are characteristic of
Ganser syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Ganser syndrome is a factitious disorder characterised by symptoms of approximate answers to questions, somatic conversion symptoms,
clouding of consciousness and perceptual disturbances, including visual hallucinations. It was �rst described in male prison populations but
is now recognised in other settings. It can be challenging to di�erentiate it from malingering in some settings.

questions.question_text:
Mr Green is a 35 year old man who is due to be released from prison. Whilst an inmate, serving a sentence for grievous bodily harm and
theft he was treated in the healthcare wing for depression and was also diagnosed with antisocial personality disorder. Which of the
following factors would be associated with an increased risk of re-o�ending?

options.text: Returning to his parent‘s home immediately following release
Having an index o�ence which was violent in nature
Returning to amphetamine use following release

questions.explanation:
Dynamic factors, which are associated with reo�ending, include drug misuse, alcohol misuse, impulsivity, relationship with anti-social peers,
