questions.question_text:
Eva has a diagnosis of high functioning autism. She has a particular fascination with patterns in music and is able to perceive and describe
complex reoccurring patterns. What description can be given to this particular talent?
questions.explanation:
Systematizing is the drive to analyse or construct systems and recognising repeating patterns in stimuli. This is a common feature of those
with autistic spectrum disorders (see Philos Trans R Soc Lond B Biol Sci 2009; 364 (1522): 1377-1383)

questions.question_text:
Mr David McDermott is a 40-year-old man with a diagnosis of DiGeorge syndrome. He has recently been referred to his local psychiatric
clinic due to concerns about his mental health. Which of the following psychiatric disorders is most strongly associated with DiGeorge
syndrome?
questions.explanation: Schizophrenia is most strongly associated, with up to 30% of those with DiGeorge syndrome developing a psychotic illness.

questions.question_text:
In your CAMHS clinic you are seeing Skye, a 3-year-old child with developmental delay. Her mother reports she had hypocalcaemia soon
after she was born. Which ONE of the following syndromes are associated with neonatal hypocalcaemia?
questions.explanation:
In DiGeorge syndrome neonatal hypocalcaemia can result from hypoparathyroidism secondary to parathyroid aplasia or hypoplasia. The
other disorders listed are not associated with neonatal hypocalcaemia. (References: Carpenter et al, 2017. Etiology of neonatal
hypocalcaemia.

questions.question_text:
John is a young man with fragile X whom you are seeing in the learning disabilities service. He has been assessed by the speech and
language therapist and you are reading the report. Which of the following speech or cognitive problems would NOT be usually observed in
Fragile X syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The types of atypical language most often seen in Fragile X syndrome in conversational interactions include tangential language,
perseverative language, repetitive speech and tendency toward delayed echolalia. Short bursts of speech with disruptions in the �ow,
including repetitions of sounds, words, and phrases are often heard. Fragile X speech has been described as "cluttered". Syntax
(arrangement of words and phrases) is usually appropriate for mental age; a high receptive vocabulary score is usually seen, and auditory
sensory and processing skills are weak. (Ref: Cornish K, Sudhalter V, Turk J. Attention and language in fragile X. Mental retardation and
developmental disabilities research reviews. 2004 Feb;10(1):11-6).

questions.question_text:
Mrs Hildebrand has brought her daughter with Down Syndrome to see you in the CAMHS clinic. She is wanting to know her daughter‘s
prognosis in terms of intelligence and potential functioning. Which ONE of the following Down Syndrome variants may have the best
potential to attain a higher IQ than the others?
questions.explanation:
Individuals with mosaicism have variable proportions of normal and abnormal cells. One study has found that the levels of trisomy cells in
buccal mucosa is associated with IQ. Those with a fewer number of trisomy cells had a higher IQ. Therefore, those with mosaicism may (but
will not necessarily) have the potential to approach normal IQ. Trisomy 13 is Patau syndrome and not Down Syndrome. (References:
Papavassiliou P, York TP, Gursoy N, Hill G, Nicely LV, Sundaram U, McClain A, Aggen SH, Eaves L, Riley B, Jackson-Cook C. The phenotype of
persons having mosaicism for trisomy 21/Down syndrome re�ects the percentage of trisomic cells present in di�erent tissues. American
journal of medical genetics Part A. 2009 Apr;149(4):573-83)

questions.question_text:
You are seeing Mr Basu who is 22 years old and has Down‘s Syndrome. His mother reports great di�culty in arranging for him to have
cataract surgery. Both mother and son speak Bengali. Based on research which of the following has NOT been reported as a barrier for
people with intellectual disabilities to access healthcare services?

options.text: Failure of services to make reasonable adjustments

questions.explanation:
A recent qualitative study has looked at the barriers patients with intellectual disabilities face in accessing health care. Interviews were
conducted with patient carers. They reported accounts of negative sta� attitudes and behaviour, failure of services to make reasonable
adjustments. Other barriers included problems with communication, and accessing services because of lack of knowledge of local services
and service eligibility issues; lack of support and involvement of carers; and language problems in participants from minority ethnic groups.
(Ref: Ali A, Scior K, Ratti V, Strydom A, King M, Hassiotis A. Discrimination and other barriers to accessing health care: perspectives of patients
with mild and moderate intellectual disability and their carers. PloS one. 2013 Aug 12;8(8):e70855.)

questions.question_text:
Mrs Claremont is a 30-year-old woman who is currently 10 weeks pregnant. She is wondering about the probability of a woman of her age
having a child with Down‘s Syndrome. What is the probability of a woman of the age of 30 having a child with Down‘s Syndrome?
questions.explanation:
A 30-year-old woman has a roughly 1/900 probability of having a baby with Down‘s syndrome. For a 25 year old, this is about 1/1200, by 35,
the risk has increased to 1/350, by age 40 it is 1/100 and by 49 it is 1/10.

questions.question_text:
Mr O'Mahony has had Parkinson's disease for 2 years and has now been diagnosed with Parkinson's dementia. He has recently started
experiencing distressing visual hallucinations after having seen his neurologist last week. What would be the �rst line management strategy
for new psychotic symptoms in someone with Parkinson's dementia?

options.text: Review Parkinson's medications and consider reducing in consultation with neurologist

correct_answer.text: Review Parkinson's medications and consider reducing in consultation with neurologist

questions.explanation:
The NICE guidelines for Parkinson's disease state that the �rst course of action in new hallucinations is to reduce the dosage of any
Parkinson's disease medicines that might have triggered hallucinations or delusions, taking into account the severity of symptoms and
possible withdrawal e�ects. Seek advice from a healthcare professional with specialist expertise in Parkinson's disease before modifying
therapy. Haloperidol is contraindicated in Parkinson's disease for its potential to worsen Parkinsonism and cause life threatening extra
pyramidal side e�ects. Lithium is not indicated. Quetiapine may be considered if the symptoms are distressing and do not respond to other
treatments. However, if Mr O'Mahony is not yet on a cholinesterase inhibitor this would the best medication to start prior to adding
antipsychotics. (Ref: Parkinson's disease in adults. NICE guideline [NG71] Published date: July
2017.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Brenda Yung is a 82 year old woman with a diagnosis of mild Alzheimer' disease who wishes to remain in her home as long as possible.
Her family is keen for her to move to a residential home. They are querying her capacity to make a decision around this. Which of the
following is not true regarding mental capacity?

options.text: It can be enhanced by repeated discussions
It can only be assessed by a psychiatrist
It applies to general decisions about every day issues
It can vary and be present at sometimes and not at others
It may be impaired for one decision but not another

correct_answer.text: It can only be assessed by a psychiatrist

questions.explanation:
Mental capacity does not have to be assessed by a psychiatrist. A wide variety of healthcare and legal professionals should be able to assess
capacity, particularly with reference to their speci�c professional roles. Psychiatrists can be asked to assist if the decision is di�cult or
contentious.

questions.question_text: What is the �rst line medication for a patient newly diagnosed with mild-moderate Lewy Body Dementia?
questions.explanation:
The NICE guidelines state the following: O�er donepezil or rivastigmine to people with mild to moderate dementia with Lewy Bodies. Only
consider galantamine for the above patient group if donepezil or rivastigmine are not tolerated. Consider memantine for people with
dementia with Lewy bodies if AChE inhibitors are not tolerated or are contraindicated. Trazadone is an antidepressant and not a �rst line
treatment for dementia. Quetiapine is not indicated as there are no psychotic symptoms reported, and even if there were, an AChE inhibitor
would be the �rst line of treatment. (Reference: Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their
carers. NICE guideline [NG97] Published date: June 2018. non-cognitive-symptoms)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a core feature of dementia with Lewy bodies?
questions.explanation:
In addition to cognitive decline (dementia), a patient with probable Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB) must also have at least two “core
clinical features" which includes: cognitive �uctuations, visual hallucinations, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder, and
parkinsonism. Other features such as antipsychotic sensitivity, falls, hallucinations in other modalities, delusions, anxiety and depression
may be supportive but are not core features. (Ref: Farlow RF, DeKosky ST, Eichler AF. (2018) Clinical features and diagnosis of dementia with
Lewy bodies.

questions.question_text:
Mabel is 82 years old and lives alone. She has recently been diagnosed with late onset schizophrenia (or paraphrenia). Which ONE of the
following symptoms are more commonly found in late onset schizophrenia when compared to adult onset schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
A few studies have compared early onset and late onset schizophrenia (previously known as paraphrenia) with adult onset schizophrenia
identifying signi�cant di�erences in phenomenology and symptomatology. Persecutory delusions and partition delusions are more common
in late onset schizophrenia. Catatonia, thought insertion and withdrawal are more common in young onset as are negative symptoms such
as blunting of a�ect. Formal thought disorder is also more common in younger age groups. (Ref: Howard R, Castle D, Wessely S, Murray R. A
comparative study of 470 cases of early-onset and late-onset schizophrenia. The British journal of psychiatry. 1993 Sep;163(3):352-7)

questions.question_text:
Miss Laura Brookes is a 55-year-old woman who has been diagnosed with REM sleep disorder due to excessive movements during sleep.
Which of the following is this diagnosis associated with?
questions.explanation:
REM sleep behavioural disorder is characterized by patients acting out their dreams during REM sleep and involves the loss of normal
muscle tone during this phase of sleep. It is strongly associated with later development of synucleopathies, such as Parkinson's disease and
Lewy Body Dementia.

questions.question_text:
Depression is commonly co-morbid with dementia but can be more di�cult to identify in patients with clinically signi�cant cognitive
impairment. Which of the followings are most useful for detecting depression in people with dementia?
questions.explanation:
The Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia is designed for the assessment of depression in older people with dementia who can at least
communicate basic needs. It has been tested for reliability, sensitivity and validity on patients in community, hospital and care home
settings. Scores are determined by a combination of prior observation and two interviews: 20 minutes with the carer and 10 minutes with
the patient.

questions.question_text:
You have just diagnosed Mr Jackson with mixed Alzheimer's and vascular dementia in the memory clinic. His daughter phones you
afterwards to inquire about risk factors she might address to reduce her chance of developing dementia. Which ONE of the following
statements is INCORRECT with regards to associations with dementia?

options.text: Obesity associated with increased risk for Alzheimer's dementia
Reduced frequency of social contacts associated with increased risk of all types of dementia
Late life depression associated with increased risk of all types of dementia
Type 2 diabetes associated with increased risk of vascular dementia
Rural living associated with increased risk of Alzheimer's dementia

correct_answer.text: Rural living associated with increased risk of Alzheimer's dementia

questions.explanation:
A recent review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses examined associations between 76 factors and dementia. Seven associations
presented convincing evidence. These were benzodiazepine use, depression at any age, late life depression, frequency of social contacts for
all types of dementia. Type 2 diabetes was associated with vascular dementia and Alzheimer's disease. Obesity has previously been
associated with Alzheimer's dementia. Rural living was found to not be signi�cant in terms of association with dementia of any type. (Ref:
Bellou V, Belbasis L, Tzoulaki I, Middleton LT, Ioannidis JP, Evangelou E. Systematic evaluation of the associations between environmental risk
factors and dementia: An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Alzheimer's & Dementia. 2017 Apr 1;13(4):406-18.)

questions.question_text: Regarding suicide in later life, which ONE of the following interventions is correctly matched to its type of preventative strategy?

options.text: Restriction of lethal means of suicide – indicated prevention
ECT for inpatients with psychotic depression – selective intervention
Peer companionship and befriending programs for isolated older people – universal prevention
Education program to improve GP's ability to treat depression – universal prevention
Proactive screening for depression and pain management in older adults in primary care with poorly controlled pain – selective

questions.explanation:
Universal prevention aims to reduce incidence at whole community or society levels. Selective prevention targets groups who do not
currently have suicidal ideation but are vulnerable due to life circumstances or demonstrate risk factors for depression and suicide.
Indicated prevention focusses on individuals who are in imminent danger of attempting suicide, have recently done so, or express suicidal
thoughts. Restriction of lethal means is a universal prevention. Education programs to improve GP's treatment is a selective prevention as it
focusses on patients who are already diagnosed with depression. Peer companionship for isolated older people is a selective intervention as
it targets lonely people who are at higher risk of suicide. ECT for inpatients with psychotic depression is an indicated prevention strategy as it
targets those who are high risk of suicide. Proactive screening for depression of older adults with uncontrolled pain is a selective
intervention as it targets a group who do not necessarily have depression but have pain which is a risk factor for developing depression and
attempting suicide. (Ref: Lapierre S, Erlangsen A, Waern M, De Leo D, Oyama H, Scocco P, et al. A systematic review of elderly suicide
prevention programs. Crisis. 2011;32(2):88-98)

questions.question_text:
Mr Jones is a 65-year-old man who is brought to A&E with a sudden onset of severe headache, vomiting, and dizziness, after having had a
brief loss of consciousness whilst in the supermarket. He has a pacemaker and history of hypertension. Which investigation would be the
initial priority in his emergency management?
questions.explanation:
CT brain is the most important initial investigation for this gentleman who may have a sub-arachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). The cornerstone
of SAH diagnosis is the noncontrast head CT scan. The sensitivity of head CT for detecting SAH is highest in the �rst 6 to 12 hours after SAH
(nearly 100%) and then progressively declines over time to about 58% at day �ve. MRI is also sensitive but would be contraindicated because
of his pacemaker. An echocardiogram is not the most important investigation at this point, nor is a chest X-ray. A lumbar puncture would be
appropriate if the CT head was negative and there was still a high suspicion of a subarachnoid haemorrhage. (Ref: Vermeulen M, van Gijn J.
The diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry. 1990;53(5):365-372)

questions.question_text:
Mr Evans has been referred to secondary care mental health services by his GP. He has read about repetitive Transcranial Magnetic
Stimulation and would like to try it. NICE supports the use of rTMS for which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Evidence on repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for depression shows no major safety concerns. The evidence on its e�cacy in the
short term is adequate, although the clinical response is variable. Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for depression may be used
with normal arrangements for clinical governance and audit. (Ref:

questions.question_text:
Mr. Gordon is a 65-year-old man who, over the past 2 years, has been making simple mistakes in his work as an accountant and has now
started to impulsively shout at his colleagues and appears very 'moody' in response to minor irritations. He does not believe there is
anything wrong with his behavior. Which of the following is most likely to be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to represent frontal lobe dementia as his social behaviour has coarsened, he is making errors at work, which are likely due
to executive dysfunction, and he has no insight into his di�culties. Huntington's is unlikely due to his age and lack of motor symptoms.
There is no indication of mood symptoms or memory impairment, nor is there any �uctuation in functioning.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Hornbeak is an 80-year-old woman with a diagnosis of dementia. Over the last 9 months her family has noted that she has been low in
mood and she has recently been diagnosed with a depressive episode. In which of the following dementia types is co-morbid depression
most prevalent?
questions.explanation:
Vascular dementia can be associated with depression in around 40-50% of cases. Huntington's disease and Parkinson's dementia are also
associated with increased rates of depressive illness.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Patterson is a 66-year-old woman who has presented with evidence of dementia. She has a personal history of severe migraine and a
strong family history of stroke and early onset dementia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Mrs. Patterson is a 66-year-old
woman who has presented with evidence of dementia. She has a personal history of severe migraine and a strong family history of stroke
and early onset dementia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Mrs. Patterson is a 66-year-old woman who has presented
with evidence of dementia. She has a personal history of severe migraine and a strong family history of stroke and early onset dementia.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
CADASIL (Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopthy) is an inherited condition caused by
abnormalities on the NOTCH-3 gene on the short arm of Chromosome 19. It is characterised by an autosomal dominant pattern of
inheritance with e�ected individuals experiencing migraines and then TIAs and CVAs around the age of 50 onwards. Mitochondrial
encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) is a condition that a�ects many of the body's systems, particularly the
brain, nervous system and muscles.

questions.question_text:
Mr Tetley is an 81-year-old man who has been referred to your outpatient clinic. He and his family have noticed that he is experiencing
di�culties with his memory and has started to have unexplained falls with some rigidity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to be dementia with Lewy Bodies in view of the early cognitive impairment and history of falls and rigidity. The other listed
disorders do have cognitive impairment as a feature, although it is often later in the course of the illness.

questions.question_text:
Mr. Owsley is a 60-year-old man who has presented with a number of cognitive impairments and has been diagnosed with a non-
degenerative dementia. Which of the following is an example of a non- degenerative dementia?
questions.explanation:
Alcoholic dementia is a non-degenerative process as the damage caused ceases once alcohol is no longer being consumed. The other
disorders listed are degenerative and progressive. Other examples of non-degenerative dementia include: cancer with or without brain
metastases; normal-pressure hydrocephalus; subdural haematoma; hypothyroidism; vitamin B12 de�ciency; and neurosyphilis.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Terry is a 78-year-old woman who has recently been diagnosed with mild Alzheimer's dementia. She is aware of the diagnosis and is
keen to start treatment. She has recently been started on Donepezil after the bene�ts and risks were explained to her. Which of the
following physiological parameters is the most important to monitor in her case?
questions.explanation:
Donepezil can be associated with bradycardia, heart block and syncope. Heart rate must be monitored when this medication is started and
when the dose is increased.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Brown is a 72-year-old lady who has recently been diagnosed with lung cancer whilst on the medical ward. The geriatrician looking after
her is seeing if it is possible to rationalise her medication from her notes. She has been on a long-term prescription of diazepam 5mg BD
from her GP. The indication for this is not clear. Which of the following diagnoses are associated with prescription benzodiazepine use in
older people?
questions.explanation:
According to the below study female sex, mild cognitive impairment, depression, panic disorder and suicidal ideation were associated with
benzodiazepine dependence in community dwelling older people. (Ref: Voyer P, Preville M, Roussel ME, Berbiche D, Beland SG. Factors
associated with benzodiazepine dependence among community-dwelling seniors, J Community Health Nurs , 2009, vol. 26 (pg. 101-13))

questions.question_text:
The Driving Vehicle Licensing Agency (UK) requests that they are informed if people are diagnosed with certain mental illnesses as these
may impact on their ability to drive. Which of the following diagnoses is most commonly associated with dangerous driving?
questions.explanation:
Dementia, except potentially in the very early stages, is associated with signi�cant risks around driving and the DVLA generally advises that
people stop driving after they receive a diagnosis. The other disorders listed can be associated with dangerous driving but this is dependent
upon the symptoms an individual experience, whether they are experiencing an episode of illness.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Larkin attends the diagnostic memory clinic with her husband. She is 55 years old and currently working as a teacher but has noticed
that she is �nding it increasingly di�cult to plan lessons and has lost her con�dence in social situations. Her husband has noticed she is
repetitive and is worried because she got lost driving to their holiday house despite usually knowing the route well. What is the most
common neurodegenerative disorder in those aged less than 65 years?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of young onset dementia (ie: in those aged 30 - 64) is Alzheimer's disease, followed by vascular, followed by
frontotemporal, alcohol related, dementia with Lewy bodies, and Huntington's disease. (Ref: Sampson EL, Warren JD, Rossor MN. Young
onset dementia. Postgraduate Medical Journal 2004;80:125-139).

questions.question_text:
Mrs Jones is a retired science teacher and her husband has recently been diagnosed with dementia. She is interested to know how his
dementia is classi�ed. Which of the following dementia is correctly matched with the brain area it a�ects in the initial stages of the disease
process?
questions.explanation:
Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia are both cortical. Vascular dementia, Progressive Supranuclear Palsy, Huntington's
disease, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease and hydrocephalus are sub-cortical. Dementia with Lewy bodies is considered to be cortico-
subcortical (Mixed type) (Ref: Shaik, S. S. and Varma, A. R. (2012), Di�erentiating the dementias: a neurological approach. Prog. Neurol.
Psychiatry, 16: 11-18. doi:10.1002/pnp.224

questions.question_text: The type of family therapy that depends on transactions is:
questions.explanation:
A family establishes a set of rules for its daily functioning through its transactions. According to structural family therapy, these rules form a
family unit's structure.

questions.question_text:
Natasha has been referred to the Adolescent Mental Health Team following an episode of self-harm in which she used a razor to
super�cially lacerate her thighs. On further exploration, she tells you that her boyfriend had recently broken up with her, and she has been
feeling terrible about herself. She describes to you her struggles with intense, �uctuating emotions, identity confusion, impulsivity and
frequent suicidal ideation. This has been going on for a few years and makes it di�cult for her to maintain friendships. She asks you if there
are any interventions that have good evidence of helping young people with di�culties similar to her own. You recommend:
questions.explanation:
Even though there is some evidence of e�cacy in the treatment of features of Borderline Personality Disorder with other therapies, the
strongest evidence for its use in adolescence is for Dialectical Behavioural Therapy where it is associated with an improvement in suicidality,
non-suicidal self-injurious behaviour, emotional dysregulation and depression from the beginning of the therapy to the one-year follow-up
(Child and Adolesc Psych and Ment Health 2011; 5:3)

questions.question_text:
Mrs Galloway's husband died of lung cancer 12 months ago. He had been severely unwell for two months prior to his death. She has come
to see you and describes her struggles to you. Which of the following features is most suggestive of depression?
questions.explanation:
An excessive guilt feeling is most suggestive of depression.
Feelings of guilt can be normal, after the death of someone close. But if they are strong and prolonged, then it is suggestive of depressive
reaction. Visual hallucinations may also be part of normal grief, but if they are frequent, persistent, and disruptive to functioning then a
psychotic illness should be considered.

questions.question_text:
Maria is a 22-year-old woman who tells you about her impulse to turn the light switch on and o� seventeen times every time she leaves a
room. She says that if she doesn't do it, she fears an explosion might happen and her family will be severely injured. Maria says that given
that such an explosion hasn't happened, the repetitive behaviour must be working. What defence mechanism is most associated with OCD?
questions.explanation:
Described by Skinner, and part of operant conditioning, negative reinforcement is a behaviour that is strengthened by avoiding a potential
negative outcome. In this case Maria thinks that by switching the light on and o� a number of times she is preventing injury occurring to her
family.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Holloways' husband died of cardiac failure 3 months ago. She is grieving for the loss of her husband. Which of the following is a feature
of normal grief reaction?

options.text: Visual hallucinations other than the deceased
Pining or searching for the deceased
Auditory hallucinations other than the deceased

correct_answer.text: Pining or searching for the deceased

questions.explanation:
Pining or searching for the deceased is a feature of normal grief reaction. Features of atypical grief reaction include; Strong suicidality,
Inability to function, visual and auditory hallucinations other than the deceased.

questions.question_text:
Your patient reports that her coworker has got several promotions and bonuses, but she has been working in the company longer than her.
She appears resentful and is considering quitting her job. Which of the following cognitive biases does she su�er from?
questions.explanation:
Your patient seems to be su�ering from the so-called fallacy of fairness. People with this cognitive bias often �rmly believe that life is always
supposed to be fair, and feel resentful when it turns out not to be fair.

questions.question_text:
Miss Jane Lloyd is a 28-year-old woman who has presented with a 10-year history of binge eating followed by self-induced vomiting and
inappropriate use of laxatives. She reports di�culties with her body image. She is not currently receiving any treatment. Which of the
following would be most appropriate to o�er her?
questions.explanation:
NICE guidelines for the treatment of bulimia nervosa recommend that adult patients should be o�ered a bulimia-nervosa-speci�c self-help
programme or specialised course of CBT. Medication should not be o�ered as a treatment for bulimia nervosa alone and family therapy is
indicated only for child or adolescent patients.

questions.question_text:
Miss Anne Gowen is a 23-year-old medical student who is currently revising for her �nal examinations. She had been feeling very anxious
about this but has been attempting to view them as an opportunity to consolidate her knowledge and show o� her skills. Which of the
following is she most likely to be demonstrating?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to be an example of reframing, when an individual attempts to view a potentially anxiety-provoking situation as something
positive so it is no longer a source of distress.

questions.question_text:
Miss Louise Guest is a 42-year-old woman who has been referred to psychodynamic psychotherapy due to a long-standing history of low
mood and anxiety. She attends regularly for 2 months and seems to �nd the sessions di�cult although appear to be therapeutically useful.
She then writes a letter to her therapist stating that she will not be attending any longer as she feels she no longer requires their input.
Which of the following is she most likely to be demonstrating?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to represent rationalisation. The patient has been �nding the therapy emotionally challenging and, rather than
acknowledge this, subconsciously produces a super�cially reasonable explanation to avoid it.

questions.question_text:
Mr Carl Sullivan is a 38-year-old man who has a diagnosis of OCD. He was assessed and referred for CBT. He �nds himself being attracted to
the therapist and subsequently joins a gym. Which of the following is he demonstrating?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to be sublimation. The patient is experiencing an erotic transference towards the therapist and, rather than acting on it in
an inappropriate way, directing it towards a more appropriate activity. This erotic attraction is a form of positive transference, whereby the
therapist is viewed as helpful and a good in�uence but taken further. It is a relatively common phenomenon.

questions.question_text:
Miss Kiera Bowles is a 20-year-old woman who has presented with di�culties with her body image associated with marked restriction of
dietary intake and excessive exercise. Her BMI is currently 17. Which of the following should she be o�ered as an initial treatment?
questions.explanation:
The initial treatment for anorexia nervosa should be one of: eating-disorder-focused cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT-ED), Maudsley
Anorexia Nervosa Treatment for Adults (MANTRA), or specialist supportive clinical management (SSCM). Eating-disorder-focused
psychodynamic therapy can be o�ered if these options are unsuccessful or are not acceptable to the patient. Medication should not be used
as a sole treatment in anorexia nervosa.

questions.question_text:
Mr Davies is a 45-year-old man who is the sole care provider for his daughter who has multiple physical disabilities and requires full-time
care. He presents to his local Emergency Department with an inability to move his left leg. He is thoroughly examined and investigated and
no physical cause can be found. Which of the following defense mechanisms is he most likely to be using in this case?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to present displacement with the patient's stress and di�culty coping with her daughter's care needs has been converted
into a physical symptom that prevents him from functioning at his usual level.

questions.question_text:
Miss Islay is a 40-year-old woman who has been referred to psychology services for input around depressive and anxiety symptoms. She is
due to start a therapeutic intervention that involves the use of circumscribed and hypothetical questions. Which of the following
psychotherapies uses these approaches?
questions.explanation:
Psychodynamic psychotherapy makes use of hypothetical and circumscribed questions to gain a greater understanding of a patient's
underlying thought processes and defenses.

questions.question_text:
Various theories have been proposed regarding factors, which predict response to psychotherapy. Which of the following is included in
Yalom's curative factors for group therapy?
questions.explanation:
Catharsis - Releases suppressed emotions and promotes healing by disclosing information to group members. It is one of the factors
included in Yalom's curative factors for group therapy.

questions.question_text:
Miss Johnson is a 23-year-old lady who has attended A&E with super�cial self-harm wounds to her arms and thighs in the context of a
recent breakup. You speak with her about her experiences and take a history. She has presented to A&E in the past with a number of small
overdoses and has been self-harming by cutting since she was a teenager. She describes a long history of unstable moods and feeling
empty inside however she is not currently suicidal, nor does she have any plans to end her life. She is interested in �nding out more about
what might cause her symptoms and engage in treatment. What management should she be o�ered?

options.text: Ask GP to refer to IAPT (Improving access to psychological therapies)

questions.explanation:
It is likely Miss Johnson has either a diagnosis of Emotionally unstable personality disorder (EUPD) or at least traits of emotion instability. In
deciding about psychological treatments in EUPD and borderline personality disorder the clinician should take into account the choice of the
service user, availability of therapies, willingness to engage. There is good evidence for mentalisation-based therapy in EUPD. Brief
psychological interventions (<3 months) should not be used (therefore Brief Interpersonal Therapy is not appropriate), and IAPT via GP is
also unlikely to be inappropriate for this reason also. Debrie�ng is not indicated and drug treatment should not be speci�cally used for
emotionally unstable personality disorder, and would not be �rst line. (Ref:

questions.question_text:
Mr. Edmunds is a 32-year-old man who has recently left his job. He reports that he has left several jobs over the last 3 years as “they start to
hate me and then I leave". Which of the following defense mechanisms is he most likely to be using?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to represent projection, with the patient projecting his anger and dislike of work or his colleagues towards them. He then
perceives them as disliking him and leaves his work. Projection is often associated with socially unacceptable thoughts and feelings, which
an individual cannot integrate into themselves.

questions.question_text:
Miss Close is a 34-year-old woman with Down‘s syndrome. She is relatively independent although she lives with her parents. They are elderly
and her mother has expressed concerns about Miss Close developing dementia in the future and what this would mean for her
independence. What percentages of people with Down‘s syndrome have dementia by the age of 35 years?
questions.explanation:
Around 25% of people with Down‘s syndrome will show cognitive impairment, including agnosia and apraxia, by the age of 35 years. Around
75% will develop Alzheimer‘s dementia by the age of 65 years. Most people with Down‘s syndrome have evidence of neuronal plaques and
neuro�brillary tangles on pathological examination by the age of 40.

questions.question_text:
James Norris is a 7-year-old boy who has had di�culties with facial grimacing and vocal tics for around 2 years. He has now presented again
with problems with repeated eye blinking and a throat clearing sound. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This is Tourette syndrome which is diagnosed when there have been multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic present for at least a year.
Chronic tic disorder is diagnosed with multiple motor or vocal tics, but not both, have been present for more than a year, while transient tic
disorder is diagnosed when tics have been present for at least 4 weeks but less than a year.

questions.question_text:
Incidence rates of some genetic conditions can have unequal sex distribution. Which of the following conditions have an equal female:male
distribution?
questions.explanation:
Prader-Willi syndrome has an equal female:male ratio. Rett syndrome occurs solely in females. Fragile X has a 1:2 female:male ratio. Lesch–
Nyhan syndrome occurs almost exclusively in males. Incontinentia pigmenti is seen only in females in clinical practice; it is invariably fatal in
male fetuses.

questions.question_text:
There have been numerous studies into the causes of autism, which have demonstrated that there are several risk factors associated with
the condition. Which of the following is the strongest risk factor for an individual developing autism?
questions.explanation:
Genetic loading is the strongest identi�ed risk factor for developing an autism spectrum disorder. Other risk factors include: intellectual
impairment; Rett syndrome; Fragile X; immune dysfunction; maternal gestational diabetes; maternal bleeding during pregnancy; maternal
medications causing teratogenic e�ects (especially valproate); antenatal intrauterine infection; foetal presentation; umbilical-cord
complications; foetal distress; birth injury or trauma; multiple birth; maternal hemorrhage; summer birth; low birth weight; small for
gestational age; low 5 minute Apgar score; meconium aspiration; neonatal anemia; ABO or Rh incompatibility; and hyperbilirubinemia.

questions.question_text:
Certain genetic conditions are important causes of intellectual disability. Which of the following is the second most common genetic cause
for intellectual disability?

Mr Quick is a 28-year-old man with a diagnosis of an autism spectrum disorder. He manages these symptoms well but is troubled by other
mental health conditions. Which of the following is the most common comorbidity with autism?
questions.explanation:
Social phobia is seen in around 17-30% of people with autism spectrum disorders. Around 84% of people with ASD with have some form of
anxiety disorder.

questions.question_text:
Mr Edward Giles is a 37-year-old man with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia. He is taking Clozapine at 350mg daily which has
been more e�ective than his previous antipsychotics but he continues to have some negative symptoms. He has become obese after
starting Clozapine and has been found to have elevated cholesterol levels. Which of the following medications would be most appropriate to
augment his existing Clozapine?
questions.explanation:
It would be most reasonable to utilise Aripiprazole in this situation. This has some evidence for treating negative symptoms when patients
are already on Clozapine and can be helpful in terms of improving cardiovascular risk factors. Amisulpride has the best evidence for treating
residual positive symptoms.

questions.question_text:
Mr Steven Drake is a 25-year-old student who is currently studying for a Masters. He has developed a depressive episode which was treated
with Sertraline. He has been taking 200mg daily for 8 weeks. He reports that his mood has improved but that he is only sleeping 3-4 hours
per night and is still not enjoying life. He is particularly worried as he has an examination in 4 days. Which of the following would be the
most appropriate management plan at this point?
questions.explanation:
While it is clear that this patient has not fully responded to Sertraline and it would be reasonable to change him to an alternative
antidepressant, this would risk destabilising his mental state immediately before an important life event. It would be most reasonable to
give a short course of Zopiclone and then review his antidepressant after his examination is complete.

questions.question_text:
Miss Emma Mayo is a 34-year-old woman with a diagnosis of schizophrenia that is now regarded as treatment resistant after her symptoms
did not fully respond to adequate trials of Risperidone or Olanzapine. She is currently receiving an increasing dose of Clozapine but has
developed chest pain and ECG abnormalities. Which of the following would be the most appropriate management plan in this case?

options.text: Stop the Clozapine and refer to cardiology
Continue the titration of Clozapine with weekly ECGs
Continue the current dose of Clozapine until her symptoms resolve

correct_answer.text: Stop the Clozapine and refer to cardiology

questions.explanation:
This is likely to represent myocarditis which is a rare but serious side-e�ect of Clozapine. If this occurs the Clozapine should be immediately
withdrawn and the individual urgently referred to cardiology or the medical assessment unit, depending upon their presentation.
Withdrawing the Clozapine can result in the individual's mental state deteriorating and so short-term benzodiazepines or an alternative anti-
psychotic should be provided.

questions.question_text:
Mr. Osborn is a 51-year-old academic scholar who has presented with aggressive behaviour and declining memory over the past 3 months.
He has no previous history of similar di�culties. Which of the following is most likely to be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to represent an early onset dementia. Delirium is less likely due to the duration of symptoms. Depression and
schizophrenia are unlikely as they are not characterised by marked memory disturbance in this age group and there is no evidence of mood
or psychotic symptoms. Substance dependence would not generally present with memory impairment as a primary symptom.

questions.question_text:
Mr Jones is a 55-year-old man who is admitted for an elective hernia repair, which was supposed to be a day procedure. He had to remain in
hospital overnight due to unexpected, signi�cant blood loss. Although he was seen in pre-admission clinic he did not disclose his signi�cant
alcohol use (up to 500mL whiskey each day). On the second day of his admission he is confused, agitated, and shaky and appears to be
seeing spiders. Which of the following would not form a part of your initial management plan?

options.text: Pabrinex (IV or IM) high potency thiamine and vitamin B and C
Physical examination to exclude other medical causes of delirium

questions.explanation:
This gentleman is su�ering delirium tremens secondary to alcohol withdrawal. He requires urgent parenteral administration of thiamine and
B vitamins as well as chlordiazepoxide to manage his withdrawal. He should also be assessed for any other causes of delirium and a key part
of the practical management of delirium is reassurance and reorientation. Antipsychotics such as haloperidol are not �rst line treatment for
delirium tremens and may also lower the seizure threshold.

questions.question_text:
Mr Aubrey is a 36-year-old man with a diagnosis of panic disorder. He is unwilling to have talking therapy but is asking about medication
options. Which of the following would be most appropriate medication to consider initially for treating panic disorder?
questions.explanation: SSRIs like Sertraline are recommended as the �rst line medication for panic disorder. Other antidepressants could potentially be used.

questions.question_text:
Terry is a 43-year-old man with bipolar disorder and is on Lithium treatment. He is now presenting with mixed a�ective state. His recent
Lithium level is 0.8. What would be your next step?
questions.explanation:
Mixed a�ective state should be treated as manic episode. The best strategy in this situation is to start him on an antipsychotic medication. Li
levels are optimal and to increase further could risk toxicity.

questions.question_text:
Mr. Jameson is a 35-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with ADHD of moderate severity. He is keen to receive treatment due to
the impact his symptoms have at his work. Which of the following are recommended as the �rst line treatment in adult ADHD?
questions.explanation:
Medication is the mainstay of treatment for adults with ADHD. Methylphenidate is the �rst line treatment, with atomoxetine and
dexamphetamine being options if this is ine�ective. CBT can be trialled if medication does not show positive e�ects.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Kelvin is a 42-year-old woman with a diagnosis of schizophrenia. She has struggled to take her oral medication in the past and has now
agreed to have a depot instead. Which of the following depot mediations requires at least 2 hours monitoring after it has been given?
questions.explanation:
Patients receiving olanzapine as a depot must be monitored for at least 2 hours after administration. Olanzapine post-injection syndrome
has been estimated to occur after 0.07% of olanzapine depot injections and in approximately 1.4% of treated patients. Post-injection
syndrome includes a range of signs and symptoms such as sedation and delirium that are consistent with olanzapine overdose. Other
symptoms include dizziness, weakness, aggression, ataxia, hypertension and seizures. Extrapyramidal symptoms are also reported, such as
tremor, dystonia, akathisia, and tardive dyskinesia. It generally starts around 1 hour after administration and resolves after 24-72 hours.

questions.question_text:
John is a 29-year-old man with a long history of paranoid schizophrenia and recently started on a new antipsychotic medication. His baseline
BP was 130/70. During his weekly review, his blood pressure was 160/90. Which of the following antipsychotic drug is most associated with
hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Most case reports implicate clozapine with some clearly describing normal blood pressure before clozapine was introduced, a sharp rise
during treatment and return to normal when clozapine was discontinued. Data available through the committee on safety of medicines
yellow card system in the UK indicate that clozapine is the antipsychotic drug most associated with hypertension. There are a small number
of reports on Olanzapine, Risperidone, Quetiapine and aripiprazole. (Ref: The Maudsley prescribing guidelines- 11th edition; pg no-122)

questions.question_text:
Miss Lodge is a 29-year-old woman who has been referred to an outpatient clinic and brought by her family. She receives an MMSE but
performs poorly. She was irritable. She states that she has no time to complete the test and that she needs to speak to the Chief Constable.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is an episode of mania in view of the grandiose delusion she describes and irritability with the assessment process.
The other diagnoses would be unlikely in a person of this age, unless there was some evidence to support them.

questions.question_text:
Miss Newton is a 36-year-old woman with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia. She is receiving an optimum medication regime
for her and is currently an inpatient in a rehabilitation unit with a view towards reintegrating her into "normal life“. Which of the following
will be most likely to help her return to independent living?
questions.explanation:
There is signi�cant evidence to indicate that supported employment, particularly Individual Placement and Support, is e�ective in enabling
people with chronic psychosis to function more e�ectively in the community.

questions.question_text:
Mr. Vano is a 24-year-old man who has recently been admitted to a general hospital. Which of the following physical health conditions
would be most likely to increase his risk of suicide?
questions.explanation: A history of a traumatic brain injury may increase the subsequent risk of suicide 9-fold. HIV positive status can double the risk of suicide.

questions.question_text:
Mr Mullen is a 30-year-old soldier who returned from Afghanistan 3 months ago. Towards the end of his tour of duty he witnessed an
unexpected attack where his close friend and fellow soldier was shot and killed. He managed to escape but was shot in his left leg in the
cross �re and continues to experience pain. He visits his GP as he is concerned about persistent �ashbacks of the event and a sense of
being on edge all the time. This has been occurring for the last 1 month. Which features would not be consistent with a diagnosis of PTSD?

options.text: Symptoms occurring within 6 months of the original trauma

questions.explanation:
Recurring dreams, di�culty concentrating and irritability are common features of PTSD. Symptoms typically occur within 6 months (though
in delayed onset can occur more than 6 months after the trauma). Hypersomnia is not a common feature in PTSD as the presentation is
generally one of hyperarousal.

questions.question_text:
Miss Saunders is a 25-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, who has been referred to your outpatient clinic by her GP with a likely episode
of depression of moderate severity. Which of the following symptoms is she most likely to exhibit?
questions.explanation:
Depression and somatoform disorder are highly co-morbid, with around 50% of patients with depression or anxiety having signi�cant
somatoform symptoms. Nihilistic delusions or auditory hallucinations would indicate a diagnosis of psychotic depression, which would
therefore be severe. Over talkativeness and agitation are more likely in mania or a mixed a�ective episode.

questions.question_text:
Mr Mathey is a 26-year-old man who has been brought into A&E with fever, confusion, agitation and auditory hallucinations over the last
several hours. He has a lumbar puncture as part of his assessment, which demonstrates lymphocytosis, normal glucose and increased
protein. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Herpes encephalitis is the most likely diagnosis in view of the acute onset of symptoms suggesting systemic in�ammation and neurological
involvement. Patients commonly have marked lymphocytosis, increased red cells, increased protein and low or normal glucose levels in CSF.

questions.question_text:
Mr Davidson is a 37-year-old man who has a diagnosis of bipolar a�ective disorder and has been admitted to a mental health unit with a
mixed a�ective episode. He had discontinued his previous medication. Which of the following treatments would be most appropriate for
managing his current episode?
questions.explanation:
Valproate has established e�ectiveness in mixed a�ective episodes, as do atypical antipsychotics. Mixed a�ective episodes do not appear to
respond well to Lithium, in contrast to its e�ectiveness in classical mania. There is no evidence for Lamotrigine in mania or mixed a�ective
episodes.

questions.question_text:
Mr Harris is a 42-year-old man with a diagnosis of treatment resistant schizophrenia who is currently stable. He is a heavy smoker and
requires a Clozapine dose of 1000mg daily to maintain his serum clozapine level in a therapeutic range. He has been admitted to a general
hospital following a generalised seizure in the community. The medical team does not identify any intracranial or systemic cause for his
seizure. Which of the following should be done to reduce the risk of further seizure activity?
questions.explanation:
In this case, adding sodium valproate would likely be the most appropriate option. It has a broad spectrum of anti-seizure activity and does
not have a major impact upon clozapine metabolism. Reducing clozapine dose is an option in some patients but not for this patient as it
would likely lead to his serum clozapine level being below the therapeutic range. Carbamazepine induces the enzymes that metabolise
clozapine, reducing the serum clozapine level. Adding amisulpride would likely increase the risk of seizure activity, as it will lower the seizure
threshold. And if the patient is treatment resistant, they likely require clozapine; changing to an alternative antipsychotic could lead to an
increase in psychotic symptoms.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Ginner is a 34-year-old woman with a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa. She has been admitted to a general hospital due to concerns
about dehydration and profound weight loss. Disturbance of which of the following electrolytes most requires monitoring during the
refeeding of profoundly unweight patients?
questions.explanation:
While disturbance of all electrolytes can occur in profoundly underweight patients, it is serum phosphate levels that are most important to
monitor. Refeeding increases the release of insulin, which requires phosphate, magnesium and potassium. These are usually depleted body-
wide. Serum phosphate is also depleted by the formation of phosphate-containing carbohydrate compounds in the muscle and liver. If
refeeding is done gradually, these electrolyte disturbances can gradually be corrected. If done too rapidly, the body does not have the time
or capacity to respond to the changes in serum electrolytes, leading to profound hypophosphataemia. Cardiac arrhythmias are the most
common cause of death from refeeding syndrome, with other signi�cant risks including confusion, coma and convulsions and cardiac
failure.

questions.question_text:
Mr Maloney is a 27-year-old man admitted to the surgical ward following emergency appendectomy. On the �rst postoperative night, he is
seen to be restless and wanting to know if he can leave the ward. When his history is reviewed it is noted he is a heroin user, and usually
smokes daily. Which of the following is not an early sign of opiate withdrawal?
questions.explanation:
The early signs of opiate withdrawal include agitation, anxiety, muscle aches, increased tearing, insomnia, runny nose, sweating, yawning.
Later symptoms of withdrawal include abdominal cramping, diarrhoea, dilated pupils, goose bumps, nausea, vomiting.

questions.question_text:
Schizophrenia is associated with a variety of clinical symptoms, aside from hallucinations and delusions. This includes cognitive de�cits.
Which of the following is most likely to be impaired when people with schizophrenia receive cognitive testing?
questions.explanation:
Working memory is most likely to be impaired in schizophrenia. This can have e�ects upon other cognitive functions, such as selective
attention and abstract reasoning.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Manner is 60-year-old woman who has presented to her GP in a distressed state and reports that she has been experiencing a burning
sensation in all her limbs. She is examined and has investigations but no physical cause is found. Which of the following is the most likely
diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to be somatoform pain disorder, which is characterised by chronic pain that does not �t with any recognised clinical
syndromes or neurological pathways and is often associated with marked psychological distress. Somatisation disorder most commonly
presents with symptoms related to somatic organ systems, such as gastrointestinal, respiratory and cardiac.

questions.question_text:
Mr Lewis is a 24-year-old man with a diagnosis of social phobia. He has been referred to your outpatient clinic for advice on medication, as
he does not feel able to engage in psychological interventions at this time. Which of the following medications would be most likely to be
bene�cial for him?
questions.explanation:
SSRIs are most commonly used in social phobia and have the best evidence base. Pregabalin is used for generalised anxiety disorder but
does not have a su�cient evidence base for social phobia. Clomipramine could be used for social phobia, but is not preferred; its main use
is in OCD if an SSRI is ine�ective. Beta-blockers can be used for performance anxiety and can reduce physical symptoms of anxiety in a given
situation but are not recommended for social phobia. Benzodiazepines can be used to manage severe anxiety but do not manage the
underlying beliefs and are dependence-forming; they are not generally recommended.

questions.question_text:
Miss Megan is a 39-year-old woman who has a history of presenting to various doctors, including GPs, out-of-hours services and private
clinics. She is insistent that she has multiple sclerosis and that she is investigated for this despite there being no evidence of this during
history taking or examination. When she is reassured that there is no reason for investigations and there is no evidence of MS she tends to
become angry before leaving the clinic. Which of the following is most likely to be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to represent hypochondriasis. In this disorder an individual has an overvalued idea that they are ill, often with a speci�c
disorder, and repeatedly presents to health services to con�rm this. They can be temporarily reassured in some cases, but can be irritable if
healthcare sta�s do not accede to their requests.

questions.question_text:
Mr Powell is a 55-year-old man. He has been picked up by the police and taken to local Emergency Department as being found a substantial
distance from his home with no memory of going there. There is no physical cause found for this and his concentration and cognition are
intact on testing in the hospital. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This appears to represent a dissociative fugue whereby an individual, usually after encountering a stressor, will wander in the community
until they are found or they come out of the fugue. They will have no memory of their travels although they may have appeared normal to
those they encountered. Their cognition is usually normal once the episode has passed.

questions.question_text:
Lithium is a highly e�ective medication for bipolar disorder, which must be maintained within a speci�c therapeutic range to prevent
subtherapeutic levels or toxicity. Which of the following medications is most associated with neurotoxicity when prescribed with lithium?
questions.explanation:
Haloperidol, �uphenazine and �upenthixol have been associated with irreversible toxic encephalopathy when combined with lithium, and
are particularly associated with neurotoxicity, even when lithium is within the therapeutic range.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Galsworthy is a 32-year-old woman with a diagnosis of OCD. She is currently under your care in an outpatient clinic and is due to start
active treatment. She and her husband have asked about her likely prognosis. Which of the following is most associated with a positive
prognosis in the short term in OCD?
questions.explanation: An early and positive response to SSRI treatment is predictive of remission of OCD symptoms.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Vaughn is a 38-year-old woman with a diagnosis of epilepsy. She has recently presented to her GP with symptoms of low mood,
inability to enjoy her usual activities and poor sleep. Which of the following is most likely to increase the risk of developing depression
among people with epilepsy?
questions.explanation:
Complex partial seizures and absence of secondary generalized tonic–clonic seizures are risk factors for depression. Treatment with
clonazepam, frequent hospitalizations (drug resistance) and lack of occupational activity are additional signi�cant contributing factors.

questions.question_text:
Jake is a 12-year-old boy with a diagnosis of conduct disorder. He has been assessed to have normal intelligence and does not have ADHD.
His family have completed a course of multi-systemic therapy with a small bene�t. However, he continues to initiate �ghts at school, has
tortured the family dog and recently lit a �re in a rubbish bin outside his home. Which ONE of the following medications would be indicated?
questions.explanation:
Risperidone is licensed for the short-term management of severely aggressive behaviour in young people with conduct disorder who have
not responded to psychosocial interventions. Quetiapine and olanzapine are not licensed. Atomoxetine or methylphenidate would be
appropriate if he had ADHD but he does not have this diagnosis. (Ref: Antisocial behaviour and conduct disorders in children and young
people: recognition and management. Clinical guideline [CG158] Recommendations#pharmacological-interventions-2).

questions.question_text:
During your CAMHS rotation you become interested in strategies to prevent depression in school age young people. You decide to join a
local project which is o�ering group training on coping strategies and mindfulness to all year 9 students, with additional 1:1 support for
those who are identi�ed to have risk factors for depression. This is an example which of the following types of prevention?
questions.explanation:
This intervention targets all students (universal) and then students who are deemed to be at higher risk for developing depression
(selective). Universal interventions target the general public or a whole population group. Selective interventions focus on a particular group
or subgroup who have biological, psychological or social risk factors for developing a mental disorder. Indicated prevention targets high-risk
individuals with detectable symptoms but whom do not yet meet the criteria for the disorder. (Ref: Weissberg RP, Kumpfer KL, Seligman ME.
Prevention that works for children and youth: An introduction. American Psychological Association; 2003 Jun).

questions.question_text:
Bipolar disorder tends to have an earlier age of onset than unipolar disorder. How much earlier do symptoms typically begin to become
evident?
questions.explanation: The average age of onset for bipolar a�ective disorder is around 6 years prior to that of unipolar depression.

questions.question_text:
Miss Fletcher is a 12-year-old girl with a history of anorexia. She is seen in her local CAMHS clinic and referred for a psychological
intervention, which uses mirroring and circular discussion. Which of the following therapies is it most likely to be?
questions.explanation:
Mirroring and circular discussion are techniques used in systemic family therapy which works by identifying and addressing unhelpful
patterns of thinking and behaviour in groups of people, including families.

questions.question_text: In children, which of the following mental health illnesses is most likely to be co morbid with another mental health illness?
questions.explanation:
Depression in children and adolescents is highly comorbid with other disorders, particularly anxiety. The converse is often true as well, but
not to the same extent. According to Cummings et al. "Among youth with depression, anxiety disorders are the most common comorbid
mental health disorders, with comorbidity estimates ranging from 15% to 75%. In youth with anxiety disorders, rates of comorbid depressive
disorders are generally lower, ranging from 10% to 15%“. Ref:

questions.question_text:
Mr. Olney is a 15-year-old boy who is smoking a large amount of cannabis on a daily basis. He is unable to engage with education and his
family has been unable to encourage him to reduce his use or stop. Which of the following psychological interventions is most likely to be
most bene�cial?
questions.explanation: Motivational interviewing and motivational enhancement with CBT are e�ective in reducing cannabis misuse in adolescents.

questions.question_text:
Brad is a 12-year-old boy with a diagnosis of an autism spectrum disorder. He has a co-morbid intellectual disability and is in a special
school for his secondary education. Which of the below is the most accurate estimate of the prevalence of intellectual disability amongst
people with a diagnosis of an autism spectrum disorder?
questions.explanation:
There are a wide variety of estimates from 40-69% to 75%, regarding the proportion of people with ASD who have a clinically signi�cant
degree of intellectual impairment. However, it appears clear that most people with ASD have a degree of intellectual impairment, with this
being more likely in those with autism rather than other spectrum disorders.

questions.question_text:
Miss Farnham is a 14-year-old girl who has been referred to your outpatient clinic after her mother took her to the GP with concerns about
her weight. She presents as very thin and it is clear that she been restricting her dietary intake for several months. Which of the following
would be most important to perform as part of her assessment?
questions.explanation:
It appears that this patient has anorexia nervosa. It is essential to establish a BMI to establish the diagnosis and to determine the likelihood
of physiological compromise. A blood pressure, ideally lying and standing, would be useful, as would some targeted investigations,
particularly measurements of electrolytes and serum haemoglobin.

questions.question_text:
Miss Jones is a 13-year-old girl with a diagnosis of severe intellectual disability. She has been prescribed a psychotropic medication but her
mother believes that this has caused her di�culties in swallowing adequately. Which of the following medications would be most likely to
cause this side e�ect?
questions.explanation:
Olanzapine would be the most likely medication of this list to cause dysphagia due to its sedative e�ect and its blockade of dopamine that
can lead to a parkinsonian impairment of swallowing. Benzodiazepines like clonazepam can also produce this e�ect.

questions.question_text:
Shaun Richards is a 16-year-old boy who has been brought into his local Emergency Department by his father. He had assaulted his mother
at home. He has refused to speak to the police and to healthcare sta�. He is currently being supervised by security with no issues. Which of
the following would be the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
The most appropriate �rst step would be speaking to the boy's father to obtain a collateral history as no direct history is available. This
would then inform any further decisions.

questions.question_text:
Jack Young is a 15-year-old boy with a diagnosis of ADHD. He is currently maintained on methylphenidate. He and his mother have asked in
clinic about what could have caused his ADHD. Which of the following is the most important antenatal risk factor for developing ADHD?
questions.explanation:
Antenatal maternal smoking is associated with the development of ADHD in o�spring. SSRI use is not associated with ADHD, although
bupropion use is; this may be due to its use in smoking cessation. There is contradictory evidence around maternal ca�eine use and ADHD.
Low maternal folate levels are associated with ADHD. Paternal age is not associated with ADHD.

questions.question_text:
Jenny is a 3-year-old girl with global developmental delay. She did learn to speak a few words initially but has lost this ability now. She
demonstrates breathing di�culties, odd hand movements and also su�ers seizures. Which of the following disorders cause epilepsy in
childhood?
questions.explanation:
Rett syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations in MECP2 that occurs almost exclusively in females. After a period of
initially normal development during the �rst 6 to 18 months of life, girls experience loss of speech and purposeful hand use, and develop
stereotypic hand movements, and gait abnormalities. Epilepsy a�ects the majority of patients with the syndrome. DiGeorge syndrome
a�ects the palate and heart. Gilbert Syndrome causes benign raised bilirubin levels. Boerhaave syndrome occurs when vomiting causes
oesophageal tears. Down Syndrome a�ects a number of organ systems but is not associated with seizures.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Atkins is a 43-year-old woman with a current history of alcohol dependence who is drinking around 500ml of vodka daily. She has
recently developed an infection and requires antibiotics from her GP. Which of the following antibiotics should be avoided in her case?
questions.explanation:
Metronidazole inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase and causes acetaldehyde to accumulate in the bloodstream. A disul�ram like reaction
occurs when consuming alcohol and the patient may complain of symptoms such as facial �ushing, throbbing headache and palpitations. A
patient taking metronidazole orally should abstain from drinking alcohol while taking metronidazole and for 48 hours after stopping it.

questions.question_text:
Mr Bailey is a 42-year-old man who has a history of alcohol dependence. He has been admitted to a general hospital as an emergency. He is
tremulous, sweating profusely and has a marked tachycardia. He has a generalised seizure immediately after admission. Which of the
following treatments would be most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
This patient is experiencing an alcohol withdrawal state associated with generalised seizures. He requires benzodiazepines to manage the
withdrawal symptoms and reduce the risk of further seizure activity. Antiepileptic medications can be used to reduce the risk of seizures but
would not address the overall withdrawal state.
